intro: Livorno is Tuscany's port on the Ligurian Sea, a short train ride from Pisa. In its Villa Fabbricotti park, redesigned in the 1880s for the Fabbricotti family and owned by the city since 1936, a reader photographed two trees on an autumn walk and sent them to us: a wide, lopsided cedar on the lawn and a southern magnolia spreading its dome beside a gravel path.

trees.story:
Livorno's Villa Fabbricotti park was redesigned by the architect Vincenzo Micheli for Bernardo Fabbricotti, who bought the estate in 1881, and the Tuscan region lists cedars among the trees he left behind. A reader walking in the park this autumn stopped at this one and sent us its photograph.

It is the kind of cedar that grows only when it is given a lawn of its own. A single dark trunk rises out of bare earth and opens into a crown far wider than it is deep, layered in flat blue-green tiers. On the right the limbs reach out so far that their ends droop down towards the fan palms beneath, while the crown leans after them, as if the whole tree had been pulled gently sideways for a century. The drooping sprays look like a Himalayan cedar, a deodar, but we would like a reader to confirm which cedar it is.

The family sold the villa and its grounds to the city in 1936, and the villa now holds the Biblioteca Labronica, the city library. We do not know when this tree was planted or how big it is; if you do, tell us here.

Walk round to the right side to stand under the longest limbs.

trees.story:
A few steps from the park's big cedar, a reader photographed this southern magnolia on the same autumn walk in Livorno's Villa Fabbricotti, and sent it to us too.

Magnolias were part of the plan here. The Tuscan region's account of the park, which the architect Vincenzo Micheli redesigned for Bernardo Fabbricotti after he bought it in 1881, names them among its trees, and this one has had room to become what a southern magnolia becomes in a Mediterranean garden. A short, dark trunk stands on a ring of bare earth worn by feet, then splits almost at once into a dozen crooked limbs that spread out level before turning up. The whole crown makes a dome wider than it is tall, thick with leathery evergreen leaves, glossy on top and rusty brown beneath.

In late spring and early summer it carries the big white flowers, scented like lemon, that gave the tree its fame in the gardens of the south. In the reader's November photograph it is all leaf, and the palm beside it tilts in from the right.

We do not know its age or girth; tell us here if you know them.

Step under the outer limbs, where the leaves close over your head.

question_meta: Which old trees can you see in Livorno? A cedar and a southern magnolia in the Villa Fabbricotti park, and how to find them.
question_answer: In Livorno's Villa Fabbricotti park, off Viale della Liberta, a wide cedar stands on the lawn by the playground and a southern magnolia spreads beside a gravel path a few steps away. Both are free to visit in park hours.
question_context: Livorno grew up as the Medici's free port on the Tuscan coast, and its villa parks are the green rooms of the newer city. Villa Fabbricotti, on Viale della Liberta, was bought in 1881 by Bernardo Fabbricotti, whose architect Vincenzo Micheli redesigned the villa and its park; the Tuscan region's account lists magnolias, eucalyptus, cedars, figs and cypresses among its trees. The family sold it to the city in 1936, and today the villa houses the Biblioteca Labronica. A reader walking there in November photographed two of its trees and sent them to us. One is a cedar with a crown spread far wider than it is deep, its longest limbs drooping towards the fan palms. The other, a few steps away, is a southern magnolia whose short trunk breaks into a low dome of glossy leaves. We do not yet know their ages or sizes, and anyone who does can tell us on the trees' pages.

faq.q: Can I visit the trees in Villa Fabbricotti?
faq.a: Yes. Villa Fabbricotti is a public park in Livorno, free to enter in daytime.

faq.q: When does the magnolia in Villa Fabbricotti flower?
faq.a: Southern magnolias carry their big white, lemon-scented flowers in late spring and early summer.

faq.q: How old are the trees in Villa Fabbricotti?
faq.a: We do not know yet. The park was redesigned after 1881; if you know when these trees were planted, tell us on their pages.
